questiontext.text: Node Coverage (NC) is satisfied by a set of test paths when:

answer.text: Every reachable node of the graph is visited by at least one test path

feedback.text: Correct — NC requires that each node be reached.

answer.text: Every edge of the graph is traversed by at least one test path

feedback.text: That is Edge Coverage, which is stronger than Node Coverage.

answer.text: Every complete path from entry to exit is executed

feedback.text: That is Complete Path Coverage, far stronger and usually infeasible.

answer.text: Every node is visited exactly once

feedback.text: NC only requires each node be visited at least once; repeats are allowed.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage imposes one test requirement per node: each reachable node must be visited by some test path.

questiontext.text: Edge Coverage (EC) is satisfied by a set of test paths when:

answer.text: Every reachable edge of the graph is traversed by at least one test path

feedback.text: Correct — EC requires that each edge (branch) be taken.

answer.text: Every reachable node of the graph is visited

feedback.text: That is Node Coverage, which is weaker than Edge Coverage.

answer.text: Every pair of adjacent edges is traversed

feedback.text: That is Edge-Pair Coverage, which is stronger than Edge Coverage.

answer.text: Every edge is traversed exactly once

feedback.text: EC only requires each edge be taken at least once; an edge may repeat.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage imposes one test requirement per edge: each reachable edge must be traversed by some test path.

questiontext.text: Classic statement coverage corresponds to which structural graph-coverage criterion on the control-flow graph?

answer.text: Node Coverage

feedback.text: Correct — executing every statement means visiting every node (basic block).

answer.text: Edge Coverage

feedback.text: Edge Coverage corresponds to branch coverage, which is stronger.

answer.text: Edge-Pair Coverage

feedback.text: Edge-pair coverage is much stronger than statement coverage.

answer.text: Complete Path Coverage

feedback.text: Complete path coverage is generally infeasible and far stronger.

generalfeedback.text: Nodes model basic blocks/statements, so statement coverage is exactly Node Coverage.

questiontext.text: Classic branch coverage corresponds to which structural graph-coverage criterion?

answer.text: Edge Coverage

feedback.text: Correct — every branch outcome is an edge that must be traversed.

answer.text: Node Coverage

feedback.text: Node coverage corresponds to statement coverage, which is weaker.

answer.text: Prime Path Coverage

feedback.text: Prime path coverage is much stronger than branch coverage.

answer.text: Complete Path Coverage

feedback.text: Complete path coverage is generally infeasible and far stronger.

generalfeedback.text: Each decision outcome is an outgoing edge, so branch coverage is exactly Edge Coverage.

questiontext.text: In a control-flow graph, a single node typically models:

answer.text: A basic block — a maximal sequence of statements with no internal branch

feedback.text: Correct — a node is a basic block executed as a unit.

answer.text: A single branch outcome of a decision

feedback.text: That is an edge, not a node.

answer.text: A complete execution from entry to exit

feedback.text: That is a test path, not a node.

answer.text: A variable definition

feedback.text: Variable definitions belong to data-flow analysis, not to what a node models structurally.

generalfeedback.text: A node models a basic block: a straight-line run of statements entered only at the top and left only at the bottom.

questiontext.text: In a control-flow graph, an edge from node u to node v models:

answer.text: A possible transfer of control from block u to block v (e.g. a branch outcome)

feedback.text: Correct — an edge is a possible flow of control between blocks.

answer.text: A basic block of statements

feedback.text: That is a node, not an edge.

answer.text: A definition-use pair for some variable

feedback.text: DU pairs belong to data-flow coverage, not to the structural meaning of an edge.

answer.text: The entire body of a loop

feedback.text: A loop body is one or more nodes; an edge is a single control transfer.

generalfeedback.text: An edge represents one possible control transfer between basic blocks; a decision's outcomes are its outgoing edges.

questiontext.text: In graph-based testing, a test path is a path that:

answer.text: Starts at an initial node and ends at a final node of the graph

feedback.text: Correct — a test path represents one complete execution from entry to exit.

answer.text: Visits every node of the graph exactly once

feedback.text: That is a Hamiltonian path, not a test path.

answer.text: Is any single edge of the graph

feedback.text: A single edge is a path of length 1, but a test path must run from an initial to a final node.

answer.text: Never repeats any node

feedback.text: A test path may repeat nodes (e.g. loop iterations); only simple paths forbid repeats.

generalfeedback.text: A test path runs from an initial node to a final node; executing one test case follows exactly one test path.

questiontext.text: A test requirement for a structural coverage criterion is:

answer.text: A specific structural element (e.g. a node or an edge) that some test path must tour

feedback.text: Correct — a criterion yields a set of test requirements.

answer.text: A single test case with concrete input values

feedback.text: That is a test case; a requirement is the element the case must cover.

answer.text: The expected output of the program

feedback.text: That is an oracle, not a coverage requirement.

answer.text: A complete path from entry to exit

feedback.text: A test path may satisfy many requirements, but a requirement is the element to be toured.

generalfeedback.text: For Node Coverage each node is a test requirement; for Edge Coverage each edge is a test requirement.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph has nodes 1..5 and edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5. How many test requirements does Node Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per node, and there are 5 nodes.
That counts the edges; Node Coverage counts nodes (5).
That counts only the branch nodes, not all nodes.
Node Coverage has one requirement per node (5), not per node pair.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage requires visiting each node, so the number of requirements equals the number of nodes: 5.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph has nodes 1..4 and edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 2→4. How many test requirements does Edge Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per edge, and there are 4 edges.
Recount — there are four edges listed.
Recount — there are only four edges listed.
Edge Coverage counts edges (4), not just the branch points.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage requires one test requirement per edge, so the count equals the number of edges: 4.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph is given only by its directed edges: 1→2, 2→3, 2→4. How many distinct nodes appear?

feedback.text: Correct — the distinct nodes are 1, 2, 3 and 4.
That is the number of edges, not nodes; the distinct nodes are 1, 2, 3, 4.
Node 2 has two out-edges, but there are four distinct nodes overall.
No node 5 appears in the edge list; there are four distinct nodes.

generalfeedback.text: Collect the endpoints of every edge: {1, 2, 3, 4} — four distinct nodes.

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph on nodes 1..5 has directed edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 2→5. How many directed edges does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — five edges are listed.
Recount — there are five edges listed.
Recount — there are only five edges listed.
Recount — there are only five edges listed.

generalfeedback.text: Count each directed edge once; the list is the complete edge set, giving 5.

name.text: Does a path cover all nodes

questiontext.text: A control-flow graph has nodes 1..4 and edges 1→2, 2→3, 2→4. The single test path 1→2→3 visits every node of the graph.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the path visits {1, 2, 3} but never reaches node 4, so Node Coverage is not met.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: The path 1→2→3 misses node 4 (reached only via edge 2→4), so it does not visit every node.

generalfeedback.text: Node 4 is reachable only through edge 2→4; the path 1→2→3 never takes it, so one more path (e.g. 1→2→4) is needed for Node Coverage.

questiontext.text: On a control-flow graph in which every node has at least one incident edge, a test set that satisfies Edge Coverage also satisfies Node Coverage.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — traversing every edge visits both endpoints of each edge, hence every node with an incident edge.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Covering all edges necessarily visits all nodes that have an incident edge, so Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage here.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage: each edge's endpoints are visited when the edge is traversed. The converse does not hold.

questiontext.text: Satisfying Node Coverage guarantees that every branch (decision outcome) has been exercised.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — Node Coverage can be met while an edge (branch outcome) is never taken.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Node Coverage only requires visiting nodes; a branch can go untaken while every node is still reached via other paths.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage does not imply Edge Coverage, so some branch outcomes may go untested.

name.text: Why edge coverage subsumes node coverage

questiontext.text: Why does Edge Coverage subsume Node Coverage (on a graph where every node has an incident edge)?

answer.text: Every such node is an endpoint of some edge, so traversing all edges visits all those nodes

feedback.text: Correct — covering the edges automatically covers their endpoints.

answer.text: Because there are always more edges than nodes

feedback.text: False in general — a straight-line graph of n nodes has only n−1 edges; subsumption does not rest on counts.

answer.text: Because every node is itself an edge of length zero

feedback.text: A node is not an edge; the subsumption comes from edges visiting their endpoints.

answer.text: Because Node Coverage requires visiting each edge

feedback.text: Node Coverage requires visiting nodes, not edges; that description is simply wrong.

generalfeedback.text: An edge is traversed only by passing through both its endpoints, so an edge-covering test set visits every node that has an incident edge — hence EC subsumes NC.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 1→3 (node 1 is an if with no else, node 2 the then-block, node 3 the merge). The single test path 1→2→3 is run. It satisfies Node Coverage, but which edge is left uncovered?

feedback.text: Correct — the path takes 1→2 and 2→3 but never the false branch 1→3.
The path 1→2→3 does take edge 1→2.
The path 1→2→3 does take edge 2→3.

answer.text: None; all edges are covered

feedback.text: Edge 1→3 (the skipped else) is never taken by 1→2→3.

generalfeedback.text: All three nodes are visited by 1→2→3, so Node Coverage holds, yet the false-branch edge 1→3 is missed — a classic NC-without-EC case.

name.text: Minimal test paths for NC on a diamond

questiontext.text: A diamond CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4 (node 1 initial, node 4 final). What is the minimum number of test paths needed for Node Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — no single entry-to-exit path visits both node 2 and node 3, so two paths are needed (e.g. 1→2→4 and 1→3→4).
One path can visit either node 2 or node 3 but not both, so one path cannot cover all four nodes.
Two paths suffice: 1→2→4 and 1→3→4 together visit all four nodes.
That is the number of edges, not the minimum number of test paths for Node Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Nodes 2 and 3 lie on mutually exclusive branches, so a minimum of two test paths is required to visit every node.

name.text: Minimal test paths for EC on a diamond

questiontext.text: For the same diamond CFG with edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4, what is the minimum number of test paths needed for Edge Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→4 covers 1→2 and 2→4; 1→3→4 covers 1→3 and 3→4. Two paths cover all four edges.
A single entry-to-exit path uses only one of 1→2 / 1→3, so it cannot cover all four edges.
Two paths already cover all four edges of the diamond.
Four is the number of edges; two test paths suffice to traverse them all.

generalfeedback.text: On a pure diamond, the same two paths achieve both Node and Edge Coverage — the criteria coincide in path count here.

questiontext.text: What is the key difference between statement coverage and branch coverage?

answer.text: Branch coverage requires every decision outcome to be taken; statement coverage only requires every statement to run

feedback.text: Correct — branch coverage (EC) also forces the false/else outcomes, which statement coverage (NC) may skip.

answer.text: Statement coverage is strictly stronger than branch coverage

feedback.text: The reverse is true: branch coverage subsumes statement coverage.

answer.text: They are always equivalent on every program

feedback.text: They coincide only when there are no decisions; a skipped else can satisfy statements but not branches.

answer.text: Statement coverage concerns edges while branch coverage concerns nodes

feedback.text: It is the other way round: statements map to nodes, branches to edges.

generalfeedback.text: Statement coverage = Node Coverage; branch coverage = Edge Coverage. Branch coverage additionally forces each decision outcome, so it subsumes statement coverage.

name.text: Minimal test paths for NC on an if-without-else

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 1→3 (an if with no else; node 1 initial, node 3 final). What is the minimum number of test paths for Node Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — the single path 1→2→3 visits all three nodes.
One path (1→2→3) already visits every node; two are needed only for Edge Coverage here.
Three is the node count, not the number of test paths required.
At least one test path is needed to visit any node.

generalfeedback.text: The path 1→2→3 passes through nodes 1, 2 and 3, achieving Node Coverage with a single test path.

name.text: Minimal test paths for EC on an if-without-else

questiontext.text: For the same if-without-else CFG with edges 1→2, 2→3, 1→3, what is the minimum number of test paths for Edge Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→3 covers 1→2 and 2→3, but the false-branch edge 1→3 needs the second path 1→3.
A single path cannot take both 1→2 and 1→3, so it cannot cover all three edges.
Two paths suffice: 1→2→3 and 1→3 together cover all three edges.
At least two test paths are required to cover every edge here.

generalfeedback.text: Here NC needs 1 path but EC needs 2 — a concrete witness that Edge Coverage is strictly stronger than Node Coverage.

name.text: Straight-line code: NC and EC coincide

questiontext.text: On a straight-line CFG with no decision nodes (edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4), any test set that achieves Node Coverage also achieves Edge Coverage.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — with no branching, the single path 1→2→3→4 covers every node and every edge, so the criteria coincide.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Without decisions there is only one path through the graph; visiting all nodes necessarily traverses all edges.

generalfeedback.text: Node and Edge Coverage differ only when the graph has decision nodes (nodes with two or more out-edges). On straight-line code they require exactly the same execution.

questiontext.text: If a test suite achieves 100% branch coverage, its statement coverage is necessarily 100% as well (assuming every statement lies on some edge).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — branch coverage is Edge Coverage, which subsumes Node Coverage (statement coverage).

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Covering every branch traverses every edge, which visits every node/statement, so statement coverage is also complete.

generalfeedback.text: Because Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage, 100% branch coverage guarantees 100% statement coverage; the converse fails.

name.text: Why statement coverage can miss a bug

questiontext.text: A method has an if with no else; the fault is that the missing else path returns a wrong value. Why can 100% statement coverage miss this fault while 100% branch coverage catches it?

answer.text: Statement coverage only needs every statement executed, so the never-taken false branch (an edge) can go untested

feedback.text: Correct — the empty else path is an edge, not a statement, so only Edge/branch coverage forces it.

answer.text: Statement coverage requires more test cases than branch coverage, masking the fault

feedback.text: Branch coverage generally needs at least as many cases; that is not the reason.

answer.text: The fault is in a node, which statement coverage never checks

feedback.text: The fault manifests on the untaken edge (the skipped else), not in a visited node.

answer.text: Statement coverage ignores loops entirely

feedback.text: Loops are unrelated here; the gap is the untaken false branch.

generalfeedback.text: An if-without-else has a false-branch edge that executes no statement; statement coverage can be 100% without ever taking it, but branch/Edge Coverage requires it.

questiontext.text: Modeling if (a && b) with short-circuit evaluation (a decision on a that can skip evaluating b), compared with treating a && b as a single atomic decision, the number of edges Edge Coverage must cover:

answer.text: Increases, because short-circuit adds a second decision node with its own outgoing edges

feedback.text: Correct — testing a then b separately introduces extra branch edges.

answer.text: Decreases, because b is sometimes skipped

feedback.text: Skipping b at runtime does not remove edges; short-circuit adds the extra decision structure.

answer.text: Stays the same, because both forms have one decision

feedback.text: Short-circuit form has two decision nodes (on a and on b), not one.

answer.text: Becomes infinite, because of the conjunction

feedback.text: The graph stays finite; short-circuit merely adds a bounded number of edges.

generalfeedback.text: Short-circuit evaluation splits a && b into two decisions (test a, then test b), so the CFG gains extra branch edges that Edge Coverage must cover.

questiontext.text: A CFG has 5 nodes. A test suite visits 4 of them. What is its Node Coverage percentage?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 of 5 nodes = 80%.
75% would be 3 of 4; here it is 4 of 5 = 80%.
One node is unvisited, so coverage is below 100%.
Coverage is visited/total = 4/5 = 80%, not 2/5.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage percentage = nodes visited / total nodes = 4/5 = 80%.

questiontext.text: A CFG has 8 edges. A test suite traverses 6 of them. What is its Edge Coverage percentage?

feedback.text: Correct — 6 of 8 edges = 75%.
80% would be 4 of 5; here it is 6 of 8 = 75%.
Coverage is traversed/total = 6/8 = 75%, not 6/10.
Two edges are untraversed, so coverage is below 100%.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage percentage = edges traversed / total edges = 6/8 = 75%.

questiontext.text: Which single graph feature is what makes Node Coverage weaker than Edge Coverage (so that NC can hold while EC fails)?

answer.text: A decision node — a node with two or more outgoing edges

feedback.text: Correct — branching lets a node be reached without every one of its out-edges being taken.

answer.text: A node with only one outgoing edge

feedback.text: With a single out-edge, visiting the node and taking its edge coincide; no gap arises.

answer.text: The presence of an initial node

feedback.text: Every graph has an initial node; that alone does not separate NC from EC.

answer.text: Having more nodes than edges

feedback.text: Node/edge counts do not determine the gap; a decision node does.

generalfeedback.text: Only at a decision node (out-degree ≥ 2) can a node be visited while one of its outgoing branch edges is skipped, so decision nodes are exactly where NC and EC diverge.

name.text: Edge coverage requirements on a diamond

questiontext.text: A diamond CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4. How many test requirements does Edge Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per edge, and there are 4 edges.
Recount — the diamond has four edges.
Two is the minimum number of test paths, not the number of edge requirements (4).
Recount — the diamond has only four edges.

generalfeedback.text: Edge Coverage has one requirement per edge; the diamond's four edges give four requirements, met by two test paths.

questiontext.text: An edge is (semantically) infeasible when:

answer.text: No input to the program can cause execution to traverse it, even though it exists in the graph

feedback.text: Correct — the edge is present syntactically but unreachable under any actual execution.

answer.text: It appears twice in the edge list

feedback.text: Duplicate listing is unrelated to feasibility.

answer.text: Both its endpoints are decision nodes

feedback.text: The endpoints' types do not determine feasibility; whether any input drives the edge does.

answer.text: It is part of a loop

feedback.text: Loop edges are usually perfectly feasible; feasibility is about reachability under real inputs.

generalfeedback.text: An infeasible edge exists in the CFG but no test input can drive control across it (e.g. a branch condition that is never true), so 100% Edge Coverage is unachievable and coverage is measured over feasible edges.

questiontext.text: A node is syntactically unreachable from the initial node when:

answer.text: There is no path in the graph from the initial node to it

feedback.text: Correct — no path exists even ignoring branch conditions.

answer.text: There is a graph path to it, but no input actually drives execution there

feedback.text: That describes semantic infeasibility, not syntactic unreachability.

answer.text: It has no outgoing edges

feedback.text: A node with no out-edges is just a final node; it can still be reachable.

answer.text: It is visited by every test path

feedback.text: That is the opposite of unreachable.

generalfeedback.text: Syntactic reachability asks only whether a graph path exists from the entry; if none does, the node can never be covered and full Node Coverage is unachievable.

questiontext.text: What is the difference between an edge being syntactically reachable and semantically reachable?

answer.text: Syntactic reachability means a graph path to it exists; semantic reachability means some real input actually drives execution across it

feedback.text: Correct — syntactic ignores conditions, semantic accounts for them.

answer.text: They are two names for the same property

feedback.text: They differ: an edge can be syntactically reachable yet semantically infeasible.

answer.text: Syntactic reachability concerns nodes; semantic reachability concerns edges

feedback.text: Both notions apply to nodes and edges alike; the distinction is graph-path vs real-input.

answer.text: Semantic reachability is always weaker (easier) than syntactic

feedback.text: Semantic is stronger: semantic reachability implies syntactic, not the reverse.

generalfeedback.text: Every semantically reachable element is syntactically reachable, but a syntactically reachable edge may be infeasible because no input satisfies the conditions along the way.

name.text: Why EC is strictly stronger than NC

questiontext.text: Which fact establishes that Edge Coverage is strictly stronger than Node Coverage (EC ⊋ NC)?

answer.text: EC always implies NC, and there exists a graph plus test set satisfying NC but not EC

feedback.text: Correct — subsumption in one direction plus a counterexample for the converse is exactly strict containment.

answer.text: NC always implies EC, and there exists a graph satisfying EC but not NC

feedback.text: Both clauses are backwards; NC does not imply EC.

answer.text: EC and NC are satisfied by exactly the same test sets on every graph

feedback.text: That would make them equivalent, not one strictly stronger.

answer.text: Neither ever implies the other

feedback.text: EC does imply NC; the containment is strict, not incomparable.

generalfeedback.text: Strict subsumption means EC ⇒ NC universally, while some instance (e.g. an if-without-else covered by 1→2→3) meets NC but not EC — so EC is strictly stronger.

name.text: Minimal EC test paths with a loop

questiontext.text: A while-loop CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4 (node 2 the loop condition, node 3 the body, node 4 the exit; node 1 initial). What is the minimum number of test paths for Edge Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — the single path 1→2→3→2→4 traverses all four edges (enter loop once, then exit).
One path suffices: 1→2→3→2→4 covers 1→2, 2→3, 3→2 and 2→4.
All four edges fit on one entry-to-exit path that iterates the loop once.
Four is the edge count; a single well-chosen path covers them all.

generalfeedback.text: Iterating the loop exactly once (1→2→3→2→4) traverses every edge, so Edge Coverage needs just one test path despite the back edge.

questiontext.text: A CFG has a self-loop edge 2→2. To satisfy Edge Coverage, some test path must execute the loop body at node 2 at least once (traverse 2→2).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — 2→2 is an edge, so Edge Coverage requires it be traversed, which means the loop iterates at least once.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The self-loop is a genuine edge; skipping it leaves Edge Coverage unsatisfied.

generalfeedback.text: Every edge, including a self-loop, is a test requirement under Edge Coverage; visiting node 2 alone (Node Coverage) does not force traversing 2→2.

questiontext.text: A merge node m has two incoming edges, a→m and b→m, from the two arms of an if-else. What does Edge Coverage require here that Node Coverage does not?

answer.text: Both incoming edges a→m and b→m must be traversed, so both arms of the if-else are exercised

feedback.text: Correct — Node Coverage of m needs only one arm; Edge Coverage forces both incoming edges.

answer.text: Node m must be visited twice

feedback.text: Edge Coverage concerns traversing both edges, not visiting m a specific number of times.

answer.text: Nothing extra; visiting m once suffices for both criteria

feedback.text: Visiting m via one arm satisfies NC but leaves the other incoming edge uncovered.

answer.text: The two arms must be merged into a single node

feedback.text: The graph is not rewritten; Edge Coverage simply requires both incoming edges.

generalfeedback.text: Node Coverage of the merge node m is met by reaching it through either arm, but Edge Coverage requires both a→m and b→m, exercising both branches.

questiontext.text: A basic block contains 4 sequential statements with no internal branch or jump. In the control-flow graph it is represented by how many nodes?

feedback.text: Correct — a basic block is a single node regardless of how many statements it holds.
Statements are not individual nodes; the whole block is one node.
The block is one node; there is no per-statement node here.
A block of statements is represented by exactly one node.

generalfeedback.text: A basic block collapses to one node, so statement count and node count differ — yet coverage is equivalent because entering the block runs all its statements.

questiontext.text: A CFG contains a genuinely infeasible edge. What is the correct consequence for Edge Coverage?

answer.text: 100% Edge Coverage is unachievable; coverage is best measured over the feasible edges only

feedback.text: Correct — infeasible requirements are excluded so the metric stays meaningful.

answer.text: 100% Edge Coverage is still achievable by trying harder

feedback.text: No input can traverse an infeasible edge, so full literal coverage is impossible.

answer.text: The whole Edge Coverage criterion becomes meaningless and is abandoned

feedback.text: The criterion is retained; only the infeasible requirement is set aside.

answer.text: The infeasible edge is automatically deleted from the program

feedback.text: The graph models the program and is not altered; the requirement is simply reported as infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Because no test can traverse an infeasible edge, tools report coverage against the feasible test requirements rather than demanding an impossible 100%.

questiontext.text: Which edge set, together with a suitable single test path, best witnesses that Node Coverage can be satisfied while Edge Coverage is not?

answer.text: 1→2, 2→3, 1→3 with test path 1→2→3 (edge 1→3 uncovered)

feedback.text: Correct — all nodes visited, but the false-branch edge 1→3 is missed.

answer.text: 1→2, 2→3, 3→4 with test path 1→2→3→4

feedback.text: Straight-line code: the one path covers all nodes and all edges, so it cannot witness a gap.
This path misses node 3, so it fails Node Coverage too — not a witness for NC-without-EC.

answer.text: 1→2 with test path 1→2

feedback.text: A single edge is covered along with both nodes; NC and EC both hold, so no gap.

generalfeedback.text: The if-without-else 1→2, 2→3, 1→3 toured by 1→2→3 visits every node yet skips edge 1→3 — the canonical NC-satisfied-but-EC-failed witness.

questiontext.text: A CFG with a loop makes Complete Path Coverage infeasible, yet Edge Coverage remains a finite, achievable criterion on that graph.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a loop yields infinitely many complete paths, but the number of edges (hence edge requirements) stays finite.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Edge Coverage has one requirement per edge, a finite set, no matter how many times the loop can iterate.

generalfeedback.text: Loops make the set of complete paths unbounded, but the edge set is finite, so Edge Coverage is always a finite (and typically achievable) target.

name.text: Max achievable NC with an unreachable node

questiontext.text: A CFG has 5 nodes, one of which is syntactically unreachable from the entry (dead code). What is the maximum Node Coverage any test suite can achieve, counting all 5 nodes?

feedback.text: Correct — at most 4 of the 5 nodes can ever be visited, so 4/5 = 80%.
The unreachable node can never be visited, so full coverage over all 5 nodes is impossible.
Only whole nodes count; the best is 4/5 = 80%.
Four of five nodes are reachable, so the maximum is 80%, not 20%.

generalfeedback.text: An unreachable node caps literal Node Coverage below 100%; here max = 4/5 = 80%. Tools typically report coverage over reachable nodes instead.

name.text: Max achievable EC with an infeasible edge

questiontext.text: A CFG has 6 edges, exactly one of which is infeasible. What is the maximum Edge Coverage any test suite can achieve, counting all 6 edges?

answer.text: About 83% (5 of 6)

feedback.text: Correct — the infeasible edge can never be traversed, so at most 5/6 ≈ 83%.
No input can traverse the infeasible edge, so 6/6 is impossible.

answer.text: About 67% (4 of 6)

feedback.text: Only one edge is infeasible, so up to 5 of 6 are coverable = ~83%.
Five of six edges are feasible, so the maximum is ~83%.

generalfeedback.text: One infeasible edge caps literal Edge Coverage at 5/6 ≈ 83%; coverage is usually reported over the feasible edges.

name.text: Minimal EC test paths on a branchy CFG

questiontext.text: A CFG on nodes 1..4 has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3, 2→4, 3→4 (node 1 initial, node 4 final). What is the minimum number of test paths for Edge Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. 1→2→3→4 (covers 1→2, 2→3, 3→4), 1→3→4 (covers 1→3), 1→2→4 (covers 2→4); no two paths can cover all five edges.
Edges 2→3 and 2→4 both need node 2, but there is no way back to 2, so one path cannot take both; likewise 1→3 needs a path starting 1→3. Two paths cannot cover all five.
Three well-chosen paths already cover all five edges.
Five is the edge count; the minimum number of test paths is three.

generalfeedback.text: Covering 2→3 and 2→4 needs two distinct paths through node 2, and 1→3 needs a path starting 1→3, so at least three test paths are required for Edge Coverage.

name.text: Why statement coverage equals node coverage

questiontext.text: Why is per-statement statement coverage equivalent to per-node Node Coverage even though a node may hold several statements?

answer.text: A basic block is single-entry, single-exit, so entering the node executes all of its statements — visiting the node covers them together

feedback.text: Correct — the block runs atomically, so node coverage and statement coverage rise and fall together.

answer.text: Because every statement is placed in its own node

feedback.text: Statements are grouped into basic blocks; they are not each a separate node.

answer.text: Because statement coverage ignores the last statement of each block

feedback.text: No statement is ignored; the whole block executes when the node is visited.

answer.text: They are not equivalent; node coverage is always stronger

feedback.text: They are equivalent: a basic block's statements all execute exactly when the node is visited.

generalfeedback.text: Because a basic block has no internal branch, control enters at the top and runs every statement to the bottom, so covering the node covers all its statements — statement coverage ≡ Node Coverage.
